frozen_original.title: Consumer Prices Surge 6% Driven by Retaliatory Tariffs
frozen_original.synopsis: By late August 2025, official economic data showed consumer prices had surged by 6% in a matter of months, primarily driven by the costs of Trump's aggressive new tariffs. The sudden inflationary spike crushed household budgets and wiped out the savings of middle and working-class families. The administration attempted to suppress the release of the damning economic data.

primary.description_short: The supplied record alleges a 6% price surge, but its prior review disputes that figure and the packet supplies no source URLs.
primary.description_medium: The supplied record alleges that consumer prices rose 6% by late August 2025 because of tariffs, that households lost savings, and that officials tried to suppress data. A prior review in the packet says the 6% figure conflicts with cited August CPI readings, but gives no source URLs or excerpts. Treat the event, numbers, household effects, and suppression allegation as unverified; this draft is not eligible for publication.
primary.description_long: The supplied frozen record alleges that by late August 2025 consumer prices had risen 6% in a matter of months because of President Trump's tariffs, that the increase wiped out household savings, and that the administration tried to suppress the data. These are allegations from the supplied record, not independently verified findings. The accompanying prior review disputes the 6% aggregate figure: it says the cited August 2025 CPI release showed 0.4% month over month and 2.9% year over year, and says contemporaneous Reuters reporting described tariff pass-through pressure without establishing a 6% aggregate CPI increase. The input supplies no source URLs, article text, or excerpts for either the official statistics or Reuters description, so this draft does not treat those figures or attributions as independently verified evidence. The record provides no documented support for the claimed household losses or attempted suppression, and no corrected, narrower event is established in the packet. It retains the supplied date as a provisional record date only. Resolve the numerical discrepancy and locate claim-level evidence before publication; remove or attribute allegations that cannot be supported. No finding about household impacts or official conduct is asserted here.

frozen_original.title: Bondi Drops DOJ Cases Against Trump Allies on Day One
frozen_original.synopsis: Attorney General Pam Bondi directed the Department of Justice to drop or suspend ongoing criminal cases and investigations against Trump allies on her first day in office, weaponizing the Justice Department as a personal protection service for the president's associates. The cases included fraud investigations, campaign finance violations, and other matters involving individuals connected to Trump. The moves confirmed fears that the DOJ under Bondi would function as a political tool rather than an independent law enforcement agency.

primary.title: Bondi Calls for DOJ Working Group to Review Trump and Jan. 6 Cases
primary.description_short: AP reported that after her February 5 swearing-in, Bondi called for a DOJ group to review Trump and Jan. 6 prosecutions.
primary.description_medium: The Associated Press reported that Pam Bondi was sworn in as attorney general on February 5, 2025, and hours later called for a Justice Department “weaponization working group.” AP said the group would scrutinize Jack Smith’s work and review prosecutions stemming from January 6. The report documents a review directive, not a January 20 order to dismiss cases against Trump allies.
primary.description_long: On February 5, 2025, the Associated Press reported that Pam Bondi was sworn in as attorney general and, hours later, called for a Justice Department “weaponization working group.” AP said the group would scrutinize the work of special counsel Jack Smith, who had charged Donald Trump in two criminal cases, and review what Bondi described as “unethical prosecutions” stemming from the January 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol. The supplied original entry instead claimed that Bondi ordered DOJ to drop or suspend a broad set of cases against Trump allies on January 20, including fraud and campaign-finance matters. The date is incompatible with AP’s account of Bondi taking office on February 5, and the AP article describes reviews rather than case dismissals. This correction records the same-day directive AP documents and does not claim that cases were dismissed. It also does not treat the act of reviewing cases as proof of misconduct. The record does not establish which cases, if any, the working group later recommended for action or what outcomes followed.

frozen_original.title: Trump Organization Profits From Inaugural Weekend at Trump DC Hotel
frozen_original.synopsis: The weekend of January 20, 2017, surrounding Trump's inauguration, Trump International Hotel in Washington D.C. became a central hub for inaugural celebrations, donor events, and VIP gatherings—generating substantial revenue for the Trump Organization at the moment Trump became president. Multiple ticketed events at the hotel charged thousands of dollars per attendee, with proceeds flowing to a combination of inaugural committees and, through venue fees, directly to Trump's business. Documents later obtained by House investigators showed the hotel earned hundreds of thousands of dollars during inaugural weekend alone. The Trump Organization initially offered discounted rates for the inauguration, then raised them dramatically when demand surged—a decision that drew criticism as profiteering off a public civic event. The weekend established the financial template that would define Trump's presidency.

proposed_survivor_patch.title: Trump’s Inaugural Committee Paid His Washington Hotel for Event Space, Rooms and Meals
proposed_survivor_patch.description_short: The inaugural committee paid Trump’s Washington hotel for rooms, meals and event space during the January 2017 inauguration.
proposed_survivor_patch.description_medium: During the January 2017 inauguration, the 58th Presidential Inaugural Committee booked rooms, meals and event space at Trump International Hotel in Washington. WNYC and ProPublica reported internal emails and receipts documenting payments and a dispute over event-space pricing. The report said the final rental price was unclear.
proposed_survivor_patch.description_long: During the January 2017 inauguration, the 58th Presidential Inaugural Committee booked rooms, meals and event space at Trump International Hotel in Washington. In December 2018, WNYC and ProPublica reported on interviews, internal emails and receipts documenting the committee’s payments to the Trump Organization and a dispute over event-space pricing. The hotel’s managing director offered $175,000 per day for ballroom and meeting-room use, or $700,000 for four days. An inaugural planner questioned the proposed rates, and the article said it was unclear what amount the committee ultimately paid for the rental. This evidence documents a commercial relationship and a pricing concern; it does not establish the Trump Organization’s net profit, a hundreds-of-thousands amount earned during inauguration weekend, or a final determination that the prices violated law. A separate D.C. attorney general complaint filed in 2020 alleged overpayment for event space, but its allegations belong to a later lawsuit record and are not proof of the frozen row’s weekend-profit claim. The event description should remain limited to payments and price negotiations documented in the reporting.
